question: There are lily pads in a row numbered \(0\) to \(11,\) in that order. There are predators on lily pads \(3\) and \(6,\) and a morsel of food on lily pad \(10.\) Fiona the frog starts on pad \(0,\) and from any given lily pad, has a \(\dfrac12\) chance to hop to the next pad, and an equal chance to jump \(2\) pads. What is the probability that Fiona reaches pad \(10\) without landing on either pad \(3\) or pad \(6?\)
solution:
To pass a predator using jumps of at most two pads, Fiona must jump from the pad immediately before it to the pad immediately after it. Thus every successful route must include
\[
2\longrightarrow4\longrightarrow5\longrightarrow7.
\]
The middle move is forced because jumping two pads from pad \(4\) would land on the predator at \(6\).

Fiona can reach pad \(2\) either with one two-pad jump or with two one-pad jumps. These are disjoint possibilities, so their total probability is
\[
\frac12+\left(\frac12\right)^2=\frac34.
\]
Starting at pad \(2\), the three required moves to pad \(7\) have probability \((1/2)^3\). Therefore the probability of reaching pad \(7\) safely is
\[
\frac34\cdot\frac18=\frac{3}{32}.
\]
From pad \(7\), the jump lengths that land exactly on pad \(10\) are
\[
(1,1,1),\qquad(1,2),\qquad(2,1).
\]
This list is exhaustive because the jump lengths must add to \(3\). Their probabilities add to
\[
\frac18+\frac14+\frac14=\frac58.
\]
Whenever Fiona reaches pad \(7\), these subsequent jump probabilities are the same. Multiplying the probability of reaching that pad safely by the conditional probability of reaching the food gives
\[
\frac{3}{32}\cdot\frac58=\boxed{\frac{15}{256}},
\]
which is choice \(\boxed{\text{A}}\).

solutionMethods.explanation:
A safe arrival at any pad must come from one of the preceding two pads. This lets us build the desired probability one pad at a time.

Let \(p_n\) be the probability that Fiona reaches pad \(n\) without landing on either predator pad, including on her arrival at \(n\). Thus \(p_0=1\) and \(p_3=p_6=0\). Also set \(p_{-1}=0\).

For each safe pad \(n\geq1\), the last jump comes from either \(n-1\) or \(n-2\). These cases are disjoint, and each required jump has probability \(1/2\), so
\[
p_n=\frac{p_{n-1}+p_{n-2}}2.
\]
Applying this rule at safe pads, and assigning zero at the predator pads, gives

| Pad \(n\) | \(p_n\) |
|---|---|
| \(0\) | \(1\) |
| \(1\) | \(1/2\) |
| \(2\) | \(3/4\) |
| \(3\) | \(0\) |
| \(4\) | \(3/8\) |
| \(5\) | \(3/16\) |
| \(6\) | \(0\) |
| \(7\) | \(3/32\) |
| \(8\) | \(3/64\) |
| \(9\) | \(9/128\) |

For example, \(p_4=(p_3+p_2)/2=3/8\): only a jump from pad \(2\) can contribute a safe arrival at pad \(4\).

Finally,
\[
p_{10}=\frac12\left(\frac{3}{64}+\frac{9}{128}\right)
=\boxed{\frac{15}{256}}.
\]
The answer is choice \(\boxed{\text{A}}\).
solutionMethods.label: Track safe arrival probabilities
